segments.title: Gearing destroyers as the Cold War baseline
segments.body: The argument for new Cold War destroyers faced the objection that the US Navy already had many wartime ships. Those wartime designs centered on guns, torpedoes, and depth charges. The Gearing class was a capable late-war design, developed from the Sumner class, with six 5-inch guns, ten 21-inch torpedoes, depth charges, and substantial light anti-aircraft armament. Its roughly 3,500-ton full-load displacement left limited room for helicopters and missiles. Repeated upgrades kept the ships useful into the 1970s, while the original layout constrained the equipment they could accommodate. DASH offered an uncrewed ASW aircraft for hulls unable to carry a full-sized helicopter.

evidence.note: The objection to replacement procurement based on the large number of wartime ships already available.
Gearing's Sumner ancestry, service into the 1970s, displacement, and original gun-and-torpedo design.
DASH supports ASW operations from destroyers unable to carry a full-sized helicopter.
Gearing's ten 21-inch torpedoes, depth charges, light anti-aircraft battery, and six 5-inch guns, followed by the limits of this fit in the 1950s and 1960s.

segments.summary: Gearing's late-war gun and torpedo armament left little room for the helicopters and missiles needed in Cold War escort work.

segments.title: Capabilities still need deployable hulls
segments.body: Offboard mine-clearing equipment needs a suitable mother ship or a conveniently located shore base. The British example concerns equipment that would depend on an ally for transport to the Strait of Hormuz if no deployment ship were available. Owning the equipment therefore does not by itself provide a deployable mine-clearing force. The comparison introduces the postwar American problem of matching the ships already available to the capabilities now required.

evidence.note: British offboard mine-clearing equipment, mother-ship availability, and the problem of transporting it to the Strait of Hormuz.

segments.summary: Offboard mine-clearing equipment needs ships or nearby shore facilities before it can operate in a distant area such as the Strait of Hormuz.

segments.title: DASH extends ASW reach without a full helicopter
segments.body: The Drone Anti-Submarine Helicopter, or DASH, supported destroyers such as the Gearings that could not embark a full-sized crewed helicopter. It supplied an airborne ASW capability without carrying aircrew. Although light and flimsy, DASH was a useful operational system. Continuing its development is presented as a missed opportunity, given the long gap before renewed interest in drones for the same role.

evidence.note: DASH was developed to support ASW operations from destroyers unable to carry a full-sized helicopter.
DASH's useful capability despite its light construction, and the view that continued development could have improved it.

segments.summary: DASH shows how an uncrewed helicopter could give small wartime destroyers a longer anti-submarine reach decades before renewed interest in drones for the same mission.

segments.title: America inherits the presence burden
segments.body: In this interpretation of postwar naval diplomacy, the United States assumed more of Britain's maritime presence role as British finances weakened. Treaty allowances and industrial potential had not previously translated into the full American peacetime fleet that could have been built. Britain's financial difficulties included the effects of both world wars, the Great Depression, and the abrupt change in wartime financial support. The end of empires created a less settled international environment in which ships had to operate visibly in many places. Gearing-type destroyers are judged to have lacked the imposing appearance expected of this wider American role.

evidence.note: Comparison of American paper potential before the war with the postwar burden of taking on global maritime presence.
Gearing-type ships did not carry the visible status needed for the United States' new presence role.

segments.summary: The transfer of maritime presence duties from Britain to the United States helps explain the emphasis on the appearance and perceived status of postwar destroyers.

segments.title: Norfolk tests a postwar heavy-destroyer idea
segments.body: USS Norfolk combined a light-cruiser-sized hull with an anti-submarine hunter-killer role. One interpretation places the design closer to a postwar contre-torpilleur, or heavy destroyer, than to a conventional prewar American destroyer. That comparison concerns the ship's size and intended employment. Its 3-inch battery, Weapon Alpha ASW rocket launchers, and 21-inch torpedo tubes supported experimentation with postwar escort requirements. Norfolk served as a learning ship while the Navy worked out what its next destroyers should provide.

evidence.note: Norfolk's light-cruiser-sized hull and ASW hunter-killer role underpin the comparison with a contre-torpilleur.
Norfolk as an experimental ship with 3-inch guns, Weapon Alpha, and 21-inch torpedo tubes.

segments.summary: Norfolk is interpreted as an experimental ASW hunter-killer closer to a French-style contre-torpilleur than to either a conventional US destroyer or a true cruiser.

segments.title: Norfolk and Mitscher test status against capability
segments.body: Norfolk's 3-inch guns and Weapon Alpha supplied substantial air-defense and ASW capability. The diplomatic criticism is that its main battery looked unimpressive beside larger guns during port visits and official meetings. The smaller, slightly slower Mitschers carried two 5-inch guns, four 3-inch guns, and a more imposing superstructure. Their conventional armament and recognizable profile are judged better suited to representing the US Navy abroad. Norfolk is still credited with an advantage in concentrated 3-inch anti-aircraft firepower. Although cost-effectiveness is acknowledged as an explanation for cancellation, the counterargument regards Norfolk's anti-aircraft firepower as cost-effective. These destroyers are treated as status assets without yet being capital ships. Weak diplomatic impact could therefore undermine their standing even when their fighting systems were useful.

evidence.note: Norfolk's useful 3-inch battery is judged too visually modest for its intended diplomatic role.
Mitscher's armament and profile, the cost-effectiveness argument, and destroyers' perceived role as status assets short of capital ships.

segments.summary: Norfolk and Mitscher illustrate the argument that a destroyer's anti-aircraft firepower and its diplomatic impact could favor different gun fits.

segments.title: Forrest Sherman brings the new-build case
segments.body: Forrest Sherman construction answered the need to replace wartime destroyers that had endured heavy use and were increasingly difficult to adapt. Built between 1953 and 1959, the class carried three 5-inch guns, four 3-inch guns, Hedgehog, and 21-inch torpedo tubes in its initial fit. Later Tartar and ASROC modifications explored different missile and ASW capabilities, while USS Hull tested the Mark 71 8-inch gun. At roughly 4,000 tons full load, these ships remained smaller than later American destroyers. Cruisers still performed many of the fleet's presence duties, allowing the destroyers to retain a narrower role. The design also provided the basis for Charles F. Adams.

evidence.note: Forrest Sherman's design lineage and initial armament, followed by Tartar, ASROC, and USS Hull's Mark 71 trial.
Heavy wartime use, reserve-hull limitations, new radar requirements, and cruiser availability underpin the case for new destroyers.

segments.summary: Forrest Sherman construction replaced worn wartime hulls and supported Tartar, ASROC, and gun experiments before providing the basis for Charles F. Adams.

segments.title: USS Hull tests the Mark 71 8-inch gun
segments.body: USS Hull, a Forrest Sherman-class destroyer, tested the lightweight Mark 71 8-inch/55 gun. A personal preference for bringing it into service leads to a counterfactual in which 8-inch guns become standard on modern escorts. The larger shell would provide more room for guidance and other capabilities than the smaller calibres commonly fitted. That possibility remains a proposal about an alternative development path: the gun did not enter service.

evidence.note: USS Hull as the test bed for the lightweight Mark 71 8-inch/55 gun.
A personal wish for the gun to have entered service, with larger shells offering more space for guidance and other capabilities.

segments.summary: USS Hull's Mark 71 trial prompts a counterfactual about making 8-inch guns standard on modern escorts and using their larger shells for guidance and other functions.

segments.title: Farragut equips the missile-era carrier screen
segments.body: The Farragut class combined a 5-inch dual-purpose gun with a Mark 10 launcher for Terrier surface-to-air missiles. It was the first class to receive the Mark 112 ASROC launcher from the outset. Mark 32 tubes carried lightweight ASW torpedoes, replacing the 21-inch weapons of earlier destroyers. At roughly 5,800 tons deep load, Farragut had grown substantially beyond the wartime ships and retained capacity for upgrades. Its principal task was defending carrier battle groups.

evidence.note: Farragut's 5-inch gun, Mark 10 Terrier launcher, ASROC fit from construction, and lightweight Mark 32 torpedo tubes.
Farragut's displacement, capacity for upgrades, and primary carrier-battle-group defense role.

segments.summary: Farragut combines Terrier missiles, ASROC, and lightweight torpedoes in a larger, upgradeable destroyer designed to defend carrier battle groups.

segments.title: The lost volume of heavyweight torpedo tubes
segments.body: Farragut's lightweight Mark 32 torpedo tubes marked a move away from the 21-inch weapons carried by earlier destroyers. Dropping the larger weapons is judged a sensible decision for the requirements of the time. The counterfactual asks what continued development of that larger diameter could have made possible. An uncrewed underwater vehicle could combine a torpedo function with extended ASW reach, using the extra volume unavailable in the smaller weapon. That is a possible development path, rather than an existing Farragut capability.

evidence.note: Mark 32 tubes carry lightweight ASW torpedoes, compared with the 21-inch weapons of earlier destroyers.
The greater internal volume of a 21-inch system compared with the lightweight ASW torpedoes adopted for Farragut.
A proposed continuation of heavyweight torpedo development into uncrewed underwater vehicles, while recognizing the original decision as sensible.

segments.summary: The move to lightweight ASW torpedoes raises a counterfactual about retaining 21-inch systems for larger uncrewed underwater vehicles.

segments.title: FRAM modernization reaches its physical ceiling
segments.body: The Charles F. Adams class appeared while older destroyers were receiving Fleet Rehabilitation and Modernization, or FRAM, upgrades. Even during those conversions, the Navy was assessing hull condition, remaining life, and the amount of new equipment each ship could absorb. The long-term usefulness of the Gearings and their predecessors was declining. Their original designs limited the capability that could be added later. Modernization therefore accompanied a growing requirement for replacement ships.

evidence.note: The growing Charles F. Adams program and the declining long-term utility of older destroyers receiving FRAM upgrades.
Hull condition and limits on adding capabilities absent from the original design support the need for replacement ships.

segments.summary: FRAM conversions could extend the usefulness of older destroyers, while hull condition and equipment limits still created a need for replacements.

segments.title: Charles F. Adams combines missile armament with a proven design
segments.body: The 29-ship Charles F. Adams family included American and overseas orders. Using the Forrest Sherman design as a basis reduced the risk of developing the new destroyers. The missile fit developed from the Mark 11 launcher to the later single-arm Mark 13, which could handle Standard missiles and Harpoon. Two 5-inch/54 guns, ASROC, and triple Mark 32 torpedo mounts supplied gun and ASW armament. These were the last steam-turbine destroyers built for the US Navy. They became a backbone of the carrier-centered task-group force, while older ships underwent modifications.

evidence.note: The 29-ship Charles F. Adams class and the limitations of further modernization of older destroyers.
Missile launchers, gun and ASW armament, deliberate reuse of Forrest Sherman to reduce design risk, and the last US steam-turbine destroyers.
American and overseas construction dates, older-ship modifications, and the carrier-battle-group defense role.

segments.summary: Forrest Sherman ancestry reduced design risk as Charles F. Adams combined missile launchers, guns, and ASW weapons for carrier defense.

segments.title: Older destroyers buy time for a clean redesign
segments.body: Charles F. Adams construction and modifications to older destroyers gave the US Navy coverage during an eight-year gap in new destroyer construction. The chronology distinguishes American Adams construction ending around 1964 from overseas construction continuing to 1967. These ships sustained a carrier-centered air-defense force and retained the appearance needed for independent presence missions. The design critique then contrasts their crowded arrangements with listing all required equipment before laying out a ship. Establishing those requirements together gives designers a better chance of accommodating them in a less cluttered arrangement. Spruance follows this pause as a more coherent design.

evidence.note: American Adams construction through about 1964, overseas construction through 1967, and older-ship modifications supporting an eight-year gap. The destroyers also retained a presence role and an imposing appearance.
The design comparison favors establishing the full equipment requirement before laying out the ship.

segments.summary: Charles F. Adams production and wartime-hull upgrades gave the US Navy enough coverage to pause destroyer construction and rethink the next ship as a complete system.

segments.title: Spruance turns destroyer size into presence
segments.body: The Spruance class arrived as worn wartime destroyers needed replacement and World War II cruisers were leaving service. Destroyers consequently had to carry more of the fleet's presence duties. Its less cluttered superstructure is judged to give a more imposing appearance than arrangements crowded by successive additions. Its weapons included Sea Sparrow, Harpoon, ASROC, and torpedoes, with a 61-cell Mark 41 vertical launching system for Tomahawk added later. Two helicopters and a towed array supported ASW, while the ship also supplied anti-surface capability and task-group screening. At roughly 8,000 tons full load, the larger hull provided room for computer systems and their maintenance. The hull form also supported the Kidd and Ticonderoga classes.

evidence.note: Wartime destroyer replacement, cruiser retirements, and the perceived diplomatic value of Spruance's cleaner lines.
Spruance's listed weapons, including Sea Sparrow, Harpoon, ASROC and torpedoes, followed by the later 61-cell Mark 41 VLS for Tomahawk.
Spruance's helicopters, ASW and anti-surface roles, increased displacement, computer space, and hull relationship to Kidd and Ticonderoga.

segments.summary: Spruance's larger hull accommodates helicopters and digital combat systems as cruiser retirements increase the destroyer's presence duties.

segments.title: What an 8-inch Spruance might have changed
segments.body: A proposed alternative Spruance fit replaces the forward 5-inch gun with the lightweight 8-inch weapon, or fits two 8-inch guns. The preference is for introducing the larger gun on this production class. Although an initial remark connects Tomahawk VLS installation to the absence of the gun, the immediate qualification is that the ships probably would still have received VLS with an 8-inch battery. The wider counterfactual imagines other navies reacting once the armament became known during construction in the early 1970s. Possible responses include a British 6-inch gun and renewed Russian interest in larger guns. These are speculative reactions to an armament choice that was never adopted.

evidence.note: A personal preference for Spruance to introduce the lightweight 8-inch gun, with one or two mounts proposed.
The qualification that VLS probably would still have been fitted, followed by speculative British and Russian reactions to an 8-inch Spruance.

segments.summary: An alternative Spruance with 8-inch guns prompts speculation about foreign gun choices, while retaining the likelihood that Tomahawk VLS would still have been added.

segments.title: Spruance's weapons and the later Tomahawk VLS
segments.body: Spruance's armament includes two 5-inch/54 guns and Phalanx close-in protection. An eight-cell Mark 29 Sea Sparrow launcher provides a further defensive weapon. Two quadruple Harpoon canisters supply anti-ship missiles, while ASROC and two triple Mark 32 torpedo mounts support ASW. The ASROC launcher was later removed. A 61-cell Mark 41 vertical launching system for Tomahawk was a later installation. The equipment list spans changes during the ships' service, so it should not all be treated as a commissioning fit.

evidence.note: Two 5-inch guns, Phalanx, Sea Sparrow, Harpoon, ASROC and torpedo mounts, including the later removal of the ASROC launcher.
The later installation of a 61-cell Mark 41 VLS for Tomahawk.

segments.summary: Spruance's gun, missile, and ASW outfit changed during service, with a later installation of Tomahawk vertical launch.

segments.title: The 5-inch gun's automation and perceived diplomatic effect
segments.body: Two single 5-inch guns became a familiar American warship arrangement. The suggested balance combines useful gun power and automation with a visible presence during diplomatic visits. The proposed explanation for that visual effect is that a barrel appearing close to the size of a visitor's head makes a strong impression. This is explicitly a personal impression, without statistical evidence or a survey of visitors to substantiate it. The automatic mounting also provided a practical development beyond earlier generations of naval guns.

evidence.note: The two-gun arrangement and the suggested balance of 5-inch gun power and visible presence.
The explicit lack of statistical or survey support for the head-size analogy, followed by the practical value of the automatic gun.

segments.summary: The case for the 5-inch gun includes automation and a suggested visual effect on visitors, with an explicit caveat that the latter lacks statistical support.

segments.title: Spruance and Type 42 solve different escort problems
segments.body: Spruance and the Royal Navy's Type 42 entered service in the same broad period but emphasized different escort functions. The Type 42's Sea Dart system gave it an area-air-defense role that the Spruance class's Sea Sparrow battery could not match. Spruance carried two substantial helicopters and a towed array for ASW, alongside anti-surface weapons and task-group screening capability. The American class also contributed presence and numbers to the fleet. It complemented the US Navy's cruisers, including the nuclear-powered cruisers then entering service.

evidence.note: Contemporary service entry and the comparison between Type 42's Sea Dart area air defense and Spruance's Sea Sparrow fit.
Spruance's two helicopters, towed-array ASW, anti-surface weapons, screening, presence, and contribution to fleet numbers.

segments.summary: A comparison with the contemporary Type 42 separates area air defense from the Spruance class's larger helicopter, ASW, anti-surface, screening, and presence contribution.

segments.title: Ticonderoga begins as a Spruance-hulled destroyer leader
segments.body: Ticonderoga's use of the Spruance hull form underpins an objection to calling the class cruisers. The proposed comparison treats them as destroyer leaders intended to lead groups of Spruances. An Aegis-equipped ship would provide long-range air defense while the other destroyers supplied the group's muscle. This interpretation emphasizes shared hull ancestry and complementary roles within the group.

evidence.note: The objection to Ticonderoga's cruiser label based on its Spruance hull form and intended destroyer-leader role.
Aegis supplies long-range air defense while Spruance provides the destroyer group's muscle.

segments.summary: The objection to Ticonderoga's cruiser label rests on its Spruance hull form and the role of an Aegis-equipped leader for destroyer groups.

segments.title: Spruance pushes toward multi-role destroyers
segments.body: Earlier Cold War destroyers tended to be either air-defense or ASW specialists with a strong secondary role. Spruance began from an ASW emphasis but added anti-surface warfare and, after Tomahawk fitting, a land-attack mission. This broader capability marked a move toward multi-role destroyers. That change is also offered as a reason why Ticonderoga's reclassification as a cruiser became easier.

evidence.note: Earlier mission specialists with strong secondary roles give way to Spruance's broader ASW, anti-surface, and land-attack capability.

segments.summary: Spruance broadens its ASW role through anti-surface weapons and Tomahawk land attack, marking a step toward multi-role destroyers.

segments.title: NF90 collides with the Burke generalist model
segments.body: The comparison between NATO Frigate 90 and Arleigh Burke centers on a family of specialists versus a single multi-role design. NF90 envisaged variants emphasizing air defense, anti-surface warfare, or ASW. Burke offered a combination of those missions to a useful standard. The explanation offered for American withdrawal is that the emerging destroyer had become the benchmark against which the specialist frigate proposals were judged.

evidence.note: NF90 and its breakdown as context for the Burke design choice.
The proposed explanation for US withdrawal contrasts NF90's specialist variants with Burke's multi-role capability.

segments.summary: The explanation for US withdrawal from NF90 contrasts its proposed specialist variants with Burke's combination of major warfare roles.

segments.title: Kidd shows the route to Burke
segments.body: The Kidd class combined Spruance ancestry with stronger air defense and extensive ASW capability. Ordered for Iran and acquired by the US Navy after the Iranian Revolution, the ships had extra air conditioning and water-distillation capacity suited to Gulf operations. Their approximately 10,000-ton full-load displacement accommodated a demanding set of combat systems. Land attack remained limited to their 5-inch guns. A data link with the Aegis system on Ticonderogas strengthened their air-defense contribution, while two embarked helicopters supported ASW. Their combination of capabilities is presented as a bridge between Spruance and Ticonderoga and an influence on the approach taken with Burke.

evidence.note: The Iranian order, US acquisition, Gulf adaptations, strong ASW and air defense, limited land attack, and approximate full-load displacement.
Computer and sensor demands explain destroyer growth, followed by the argument that Kidd's Aegis data link and ASW helicopters demonstrated a useful mix of capabilities.

segments.summary: Kidd combines stronger air defense, helicopter ASW, and adaptations for Gulf operations, providing an example of the capability mix associated with Burke.

segments.title: Why a small order can justify a premium warship
segments.body: The Kidd order is compared with the way Imperial Japan once bought premium warships from experienced foreign builders. A navy ordering only four ships may rationally specify the most capable version it can afford because every hull must count. A much larger navy faces a different calculation: spending the same premium across a run of 20 or more ships might instead purchase several additional hulls. Those extra ships can produce more aggregate availability even when each is individually less elaborate. The Kidds expose a procurement tradeoff between unit capability and the number of deployable ships.

evidence.note: Comparison of premium foreign orders with buying the ships a large builder might choose if ordering four rather than dozens.
Comparison of the extra hulls a large navy could buy with the case for a smaller navy spending more to make every ship count.

segments.summary: The premium-order comparison illustrates why a small navy may sensibly pay more for each ship while a large navy often gains more operational availability by buying additional hulls.

segments.title: Kidd's Gulf adaptations and remaining land-attack limit
segments.body: The Kidds' extra air conditioning supported their computer systems in the Gulf. It also reduced the heat those systems imposed on the crew. Additional water-distillation capacity suited operations in the same region. After the Iranian order was canceled following the revolution, the US Navy acquired the ships and used them extensively in the Gulf. The class combined strong ASW and air-defense capability, but land attack remained limited to its 5-inch guns.

evidence.note: The Iranian order and extra air conditioning for computers and crew, with additional water-distillation capacity for Gulf operations.
US acquisition after the Iranian Revolution, Gulf service, strong ASW and air defense, and the land-attack limitation beyond the 5-inch guns.

segments.summary: Extra cooling and water production suited Kidd to the Gulf, while its broad warfare capability still lacked land attack beyond the guns.

segments.title: Hardened computing drives destroyer growth
segments.body: The Spruance and Kidd generation needed larger computer networks as sensors and other systems demanded more information processing. Protecting and supporting those computers contributed to the growth in ship size. Their components could lag behind the latest generation because developing hardened versions took time. The requirement could include recovering and restarting after an electromagnetic pulse, even when the equipment could not escape all effects. Salt-water exposure added a continuous environmental threat alongside hostile action. Electronic survivability therefore had to be considered as part of the ship's overall ability to survive.

evidence.note: Sensor-processing demands, larger networks, older hardened chipsets, and possible recovery after electromagnetic disruption.
Salt water as a persistent threat to shipboard electronics, alongside deliberate hostile damage.

segments.summary: Larger processing networks and the need for hardened, recoverable electronics help explain the growth of Spruance and Kidd.

segments.title: Kidd's later Australian interest and Taiwanese service
segments.body: Australia considered acquiring the Kidds as the US Navy prepared to dispose of them. Their air-defense capability made them attractive, but difficulties with two Newport-class tank landing ships recently bought from the United States form part of the explanation for Australia's reluctance. The Kidds instead entered Taiwanese service. By the time of the recording, upgrades had maintained broadly similar missile and combat capabilities. They remained principal warfare assets for that navy.

evidence.note: Australian interest in Kidd and difficulties with two recently acquired Newport-class tank landing ships.
Taiwanese service, upgrades, broadly retained missile capability, and the ships' role as principal warfare assets at the time of recording.

segments.summary: Australian interest and later Taiwanese service illustrate the continued value attributed to Kidd's air-defense capability.

segments.title: Cold War destroyers had to wage the peace
segments.body: The Cold War combined the danger of a shooting war with competition for influence short of combat. Destroyers had to be credible fighting ships while sustaining presence abroad. The description of that second task as 'waging peace' places a ship's perceived standing alongside its weapons. The argument for explaining sea power to successive governments is that weapons counts alone leave out this diplomatic role. Appearance and the perception of capability therefore form part of the assessment of what a destroyer contributes.

evidence.note: Cold War destroyers facing both the risk of combat and competition for influence through presence.
The case for explaining naval value to successive governments through perceived capability and standing as well as weapons counts.

segments.summary: Cold War naval presence linked destroyers' perceived standing and capability to their role in competition short of combat.

segments.title: Kidd's resemblance to Spruance multiplies uncertainty
segments.body: The Kidds are credited with an image benefit extending beyond their four hulls. Their radar fit and other details could distinguish them from Spruances, but the close resemblance left some uncertainty. An encounter with a familiar silhouette could therefore involve a destroyer with greater air-defense capability. Although the Kidds commonly operated in the Gulf, they could also accompany a carrier battle group. The argument is that this uncertainty affected perceptions of the wider force.

evidence.note: Radar and other details help distinguish Kidd from Spruance, while the family resemblance leaves some uncertainty.
Kidd's Gulf and carrier-group operations, with additional capability at relatively little additional cost.

segments.summary: Kidd's resemblance to Spruance supports an argument that uncertainty over a ship's identity could increase the perceived capability of the wider force.

segments.title: Could the US Navy have retained specialist destroyers?
segments.body: The closing problem concerns the US Navy's movement from destroyers with specialist roles toward ships able to perform several missions. One question is whether the development, form, and operational capabilities of missiles encouraged that convergence. Another is whether specialist classes remained practical only for a fleet large enough to build sufficient numbers. Shrinking fleets are presented as a pressure toward generalists, with the United States identified as the navy large enough to have sustained specialists. These questions are left for viewers to consider, without a concluding answer about whether the change was inevitable.

evidence.note: Questions about whether generalist destroyers were inevitable and how missile development affected specialization.
The claim that the US Navy built enough ships to retain specialists while smaller fleets faced pressure toward generalists.

segments.summary: The closing problem asks whether missiles and shrinking fleets made generalist destroyers inevitable, or whether a sufficiently large navy could have retained specialists.
